some of the additional stats we'll need:

# moderation
This is a type of analysis where a variable (third variable) affects the strength of the relationship between two other variables (outcome and predictor).

lm(outcome ~ predictor* moderator, data= dat)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
data(starwars)

```

## Question: Does sex moderate the relationship between height and mass? 

```{r}
lm1<- lm(mass ~ height * sex, data= starwars)
summary(lm1)
```

```{r}
library(ggeffects)
a<- ggpredict(lm1, terms= c("sex"))
plot(a)
```

## Question2: Does birth year moderate the relationship between mass and height? 
```{r}
lm2<- lm(mass~ height* birth_year, data=starwars)
summary(lm2)
```

```{r}
b<- ggpredict(lm2)
plot(b)
library(interactions)
interact_plot(lm2, pred= height, modx= birth_year)
```

# mediation
the way that x and y are related is through a third variable (the mediator)

```{r}
library(mediation)
```

Mediation occurs when there is seemingly a relationship between x and y. In reality x predicts a mediator that in turn predicts y. This is often used when discussing mechanisms. There are different ways to do a mediation analysis. Baron and Kenny is a traditional approach, but has some issues. 

Preacher and Hayes created a new approach that removes some of the issues with Baron and Kenny. This is shown in the mediator package. 
need to create two models: 
1) predict the mediator from x
2) predict y from x and the mediator 

## Question: Does birth_year mediate the relationship between height and mass? 
```{r}
starwars2<- na.omit(starwars)
lma<- lm(birth_year ~ height, data=starwars2)
summary(lma)
lmb<- lm(mass ~ birth_year+height, data=starwars2)
summary(lmb)
med<-mediate(lma, lmb, treat= "height", mediator= "birth_year")
summary(med)
```
Interpretation: 
Total Effect: tells relationship between x and y (indirect and direct effect)
ADE: tells about whether there is a direct effect between x and y
ACME: tells use where the relationship is mediated 

# logistic regression 
linear regression with a dichotomous outcome 
glm(outcome ~ predictor, data= dat, family= "binomial")

```{r}
data(mtcars)
summary(glm(am ~ mpg, data=mtcars))
```

# linear mixed effects models / repeated measures 

## repeated measures ANOVA

repeated measures anova can be used when we have an outcome that is measured at multiple time points 
```{r}
data(sleep)
# a1<- aov(extra ~ group + ID, data=sleep) this works, but not totally correct
a2<- aov(extra~ group + Error(ID), data=sleep)
summary(a2)
```


```{r}
library(ez)
ezANOVA(sleep, dv= extra, wid= ID, within= group)
```

## linear mixed effects modeling 

```{r}
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
```

use lmer() to create mixed effect model
include (slope | intercept) in the model 
- (1| variable) indicates a random intercept, where participants may have different starting points
- if you replace the one with a second variable, it indicates a random slope, where rate of change may differ across participants 
```{r}
data("ChickWeight")

lme1<- lmer(weight ~ Diet + (Time|Chick),data=ChickWeight)
summary(lme1)
```

## generalized linear mixed effect models ( glmer)
glmer(dv~ IV +(slope|intercept), data= dataframe, family= "")
- family options include binomial (dichotomous data), poisson (count data), and several others
